title: Buffer management
lead: Buffer-pool state, pin/unpin, replacement policies and DBMS control over page transfers.

sections.title: Buffer pool and pin/unpin
sections.html:
Frames, metadata and the pin contract

A page is a persistent logical unit; a frame is a location in the RAM buffer pool. The page table maps resident page IDs to frames. Each frame tracks pin count and dirty state. pin returns an address only after the requested page is available; callers balance each pin with unpin after their final use.

Several callers can pin one page, so unpin decrements a counter rather than simply marking it unused. A zero count permits replacement but does not demand eviction. A dirty flag records that RAM differs from the persistent page; later clean releases cannot clear an earlier dirty update.

PDF pp. 1–8

Pin/unpin implementation and responsibilities

pin(p):
  if pageTable contains p:
    f = pageTable[p]; f.pinCount += 1; return f.address
  f = free frame or replacement victim with pinCount == 0
  if no frame is available: wait or report exhaustion
  if f holds a dirty page: write back subject to WAL
  remove the old page-to-frame mapping
  read p into f; install pageTable[p] = f
  f.pinCount = 1; f.dirty = false
  return f.address
unpin(p, changed):
  require a matching outstanding pin(p)
  f = pageTable[p]
  f.pinCount -= 1
  f.dirty = f.dirty OR changed

The hit path increments usage; the miss path replaces only an unpinned frame. Writing a dirty victim must obey recovery’s WAL order. Pinning guarantees residency, not exclusive access to tuple bytes: locks/latches and concurrency control handle conflicts. Delayed flushing improves performance, while recovery handles crashes before data-page write-back.

PDF pp. 9–11

sections.title: LRU and CLOCK
sections.html:
Replacement policies and exact LRU choice

The source candidates have (page,pins,last-unpin): (1,0,43),(2,1,21),(8,0,22),(6,2,11),(4,0,24),(5,0,15). Page 6 has the oldest timestamp but is pinned, so it is ineligible. LRU selects page 5, the oldest eligible page.

Finding an exact minimum by scan costs linear time in frames. Ordered structures reduce selection work but require recency updates on frequent accesses. LRU favours temporal locality; FIFO, MRU, random and LRU-K encode different predictions about future reuse.

PDF pp. 12–14

CLOCK rule and starting state

repeat while searching for a victim:
  f = frames[hand]
  if f.pinCount == 0:
    if f.reference == 0: choose f
    else: f.reference = 0
  hand = (hand + 1) mod frameCount

CLOCK gives referenced, unpinned frames a second chance; pinned frames are never victims. The source starts with page 3 pinned at the hand, page 2 unpinned with bit 1 and page 8 unpinned with bit 0. The bit approximates recent use without maintaining a complete timestamp order.

PDF pp. 15–16

CLOCK request for page 10, step by step

StepPageAction
13Pinned: skip
22Unpinned, bit 1: clear to 0 and skip
38Unpinned, bit 0: select victim
410Load into former page-8 frame; pin=1, reference=1
5handAdvance to next frame; return address

The six pictures show one eviction search. Skipping page 2 changes its bit; it does not evict it. Page 8 is replaced, not the first page with bit 0 regardless of pin status. Any required dirty write precedes frame reuse.

PDF pp. 17–21

sections.title: Sequential flooding and MRU
sections.html:
Repeated scans under LRU

Assume six empty frames and clean pages unpinned immediately after each request. A six-page repeated scan causes six cold misses, then only hits. For seven pages the first pass fills [1,2,3,4,5,6], then request 7 evicts 1.

The next request 1 evicts 2; request 2 evicts 3, and so on. Every request misses because the reuse distance exceeds the pool. This sequential-flooding conclusion depends on the scan and release assumptions, not merely on the file being “large”.

PDF pp. 22–27

MRU and LRU-K

On the same scan, MRU has [1,2,3,4,5,6] after six misses. Request 7 evicts 6, leaving [1,2,3,4,5,7]. Requests 1–5 then hit; request 6 evicts the most recently used page 5. Thus MRU preserves pages needed sooner in this cyclic access pattern.

LRU-K looks at the K-th most recent reference, distinguishing repeated popularity from one-off scans. Real buffer policies can combine CLOCK with special scan handling. The source does not assert one policy dominates on all workloads.

PDF pp. 28–31

sections.title: Practical buffer management
sections.html:
Hints, prefetching and operating-system caches

An operator can hint that a page will be reused (“fix”) or is unlikely to be reused (“hate”). Separate pools can distinguish table, index and log pages. These hints use plan knowledge unavailable to a generic filesystem cache.

Prefetching pages 2–5 while page 1 is processed both amortises I/O positioning and overlaps disk work with CPU work. Incorrect predictions waste bandwidth and frames. DBMS-controlled flushing is needed for recovery ordering; relying entirely on OS replacement and flush timing would hide those decisions and reduce portability.

PDF pp. 32–35

quiz.question: P has dirty=true. What is dirty after unpin(P,false)?
options: It depends on the pin count
quiz.explanation: The new dirty flag is the old dirty flag OR the supplied dirty argument. true OR false remains true.
